longForm.title: Search and Destroy: The Attrition Strategy in Vietnam and Why It Failed
longForm.excerpt: General Westmoreland's attrition strategy in Vietnam was built on the premise that killing enemy combatants faster than they could be replaced would eventually produce a crossover point. The crossover point was never reached. The strategy failed for two reasons that were knowable in advance.
paragraphs: The attrition strategy that General William Westmoreland applied to Vietnam between 1965 and 1968 was built on a mathematical premise: if American forces could kill enemy combatants faster than North Vietnam could replace them, a crossover point would eventually be reached at which enemy strength was declining rather than growing. The premise was not irrational. It was wrong in two respects that the command structure was slow to acknowledge. The first was empirical: the crossover point was never reached. NVA and Viet Cong forces controlled the tempo of engagements sufficiently to keep their losses below the replacement threshold, and North Vietnam's willingness to absorb casualties, combined with its mobilization capacity, consistently exceeded MACV's estimates. The second was strategic: even if the crossover point had been reached, it would not have ended the war — because the war was not primarily about military attrition. It was about political will, and North Vietnam had more of it than the United States was prepared to match.

The institutional logic that produced the attrition strategy deserves examination rather than simply condemnation. Westmoreland inherited a command structure and a force optimized for conventional war in Europe, with secondary capability for counterinsurgency. The Army's training, doctrine, organization, and logistical systems had all been designed around the assumption that American forces would fight the Soviet ground forces in the Fulda Gap. Applying that force to an insurgency in Southeast Asia required either adapting the force or adapting the mission to fit the force. MACV chose to define the mission in terms the available force could execute: finding and destroying enemy main force units in set-piece engagements where American firepower superiority would be decisive. The counterinsurgency alternative — protecting the population, building South Vietnamese governance, denying the insurgency its political base — required time, patience, and a different institutional skill set. The Army's answer was to do what it knew how to do and hope that enough of it would eventually be sufficient.

The body count became the primary metric of progress because it was the one output of the attrition strategy that could be quantified and reported. The problem with body count as a metric was well understood within MACV before it became institutionalized as the primary measure of effectiveness. An enemy combatant killed in combat and an unarmed civilian killed under ambiguous circumstances both added to the count; the incentives that body count reporting created ran in the direction of maximum numbers rather than accurate numbers. Field commanders who produced high counts received positive evaluations; those who produced lower counts faced questions about their aggressiveness. The corruption of the metric did not require dishonesty at every level of the chain — it required only that the incentives consistently rewarded overstatement and punished understatement, which they did. The count that reached the Pentagon and the White House was not a reliable measure of enemy losses. It was a measure of the Army's institutional need to demonstrate progress in the metric that headquarters had chosen.

The core tactical problem with attrition strategy in Vietnam was that the enemy retained the initiative in deciding when to absorb casualties. Subsequent analysis of the war's engagements established that approximately 80 to 90 percent of firefights were initiated by NVA or Viet Cong forces — meaning the enemy chose when to fight and when to disengage. Against an opponent who controls engagement initiation, attrition works only if the attacker can force contact faster than the defender can break it. American airmobility made this possible in some circumstances but not consistently. The NVA response to American search-and-destroy operations was typically to withdraw, accept the firepower, and reconstitute in base areas across the Cambodian and Laotian borders where American forces could not follow without triggering a broader political crisis. The adversary had a sanctuary. The strategy had no answer for it.

The political will differential is the variable the attrition strategy's designers consistently underweighted. North Vietnam's willingness to absorb casualties was substantially higher than any estimate MACV's planning documents reflect. The historian Stanley Karnow estimated North Vietnamese losses through the war at approximately one million military dead — a figure that, applied to the American context proportionally, would correspond to approximately ten million American deaths. Ho Chi Minh had stated explicitly, and demonstrated through action, that North Vietnam was prepared to sustain those losses indefinitely if necessary. The American political system was not prepared to match that tolerance. Public opinion in the United States was not fixed; it tracked the perceived progress of the war, and as the progress was measured by body count and the body count was unreliable, American public opinion was tracking a fiction. The Tet Offensive of January 1968 did not expose a military defeat — Tet was, in tactical terms, an NVA and Viet Cong disaster. It exposed the gap between the official optimism that MACV had been communicating and the actual state of the war.

The alternative to attrition was articulated at the time, and the articulation was largely ignored. Marine Corps General Victor Krulak argued from 1965 that the war would be won or lost among the South Vietnamese population, not in the jungle engagements that search-and-destroy produced. Sir Robert Thompson, the British counterinsurgency expert who had directed the successful Malayan Emergency campaign, offered similar analysis to the Johnson administration and was similarly disregarded. The Marines' Combined Action Platoon program — small units embedded in Vietnamese villages to provide security and build local legitimacy — was a practical implementation of the population-centric alternative. It operated on a relatively small scale in I Corps and produced results that the Army's attrition operations in the highlands did not. The CORDS program, which Westmoreland's successor Creighton Abrams expanded after 1968, applied the Thompson-Krulak analysis at scale. By most assessments, it was achieving real results in 1972 and 1973 — after the attrition years had consumed the political will available to sustain American involvement.

Tet 1968 is properly understood not as the decisive battle of the Vietnam War but as the moment when the credibility claim underlying the attrition strategy collapsed. MACV had been reporting, through body counts and kill ratios and infiltration estimates, that the war was going well — that the crossover point was approaching, that enemy strength was degrading, that the end of the long fight was visible if not imminent. The coordinated NVA and Viet Cong attacks on 36 provincial capitals and 64 district towns on January 30-31, 1968 demonstrated that an enemy MACV had been describing as degraded and demoralized could mount a simultaneous nationwide offensive. The attacks were repelled. The Viet Cong infrastructure was, in many areas, severely damaged. Militarily, Tet was a costly NVA-VC failure. Politically, it was the end of Westmoreland's credibility and, within months, the end of Johnson's presidency. The metric had been wrong for years. Tet was the moment the error became publicly undeniable.

The analytical lesson that attrition strategy in Vietnam offers is not that attrition never works — it has worked, in different contexts, against adversaries for whom casualties translated into declining political will and declining military capacity. It is that attrition works only against adversaries who share the attacker's sensitivity to losses, and who cannot route around the attrition by controlling engagement tempo or drawing on sanctuary-based replacement pools. Against North Vietnam, the conditions for successful attrition were not met, and they were not going to be met within the political constraints that American strategy operated under. The commanders who identified this early — Krulak, Thompson, and eventually Abrams — were correct. The institutional preference for the strategy that matched the available force over the strategy that matched the actual problem was the failure that the body count numbers, however inflated, were never going to conceal.

shortForm.title: The Body Count: What MACV's Primary Metric Actually Measured
shortForm.excerpt: The body count became MACV's primary measure of progress because it was quantifiable. The problem was not that the numbers were inflated — though they were. The problem was that an accurate body count would still have measured the wrong thing.
paragraphs: The body count was a metric that MACV created because it needed a metric. Search-and-destroy operations produced one measurable output — enemy dead — and headquarters needed something to report to Washington and to the press briefings that became known as the Five O'Clock Follies. The problems with the metric were understood within the Army from the beginning. The most fundamental was definitional: the category 'enemy killed in action' had no reliable method of verification in the field. A body found after an engagement might be an NVA regular, a Viet Cong guerrilla, a civilian caught in the fire, or a combatant from either side. Counting required a determination that field conditions under fire did not consistently allow. The incentive structure resolved this uncertainty consistently in one direction.

The Army had institutionalized a reporting system in which body count numbers moved up the chain of command, with each level having an interest in the numbers appearing adequate. A platoon leader who reported low counts might face questions about his unit's effectiveness. A company commander aggregated platoon reports with the same institutional pressure. By the time numbers reached MACV, they reflected not what had been verifiably killed in action but what the chain of command had agreed was a defensible count given the pressure to demonstrate progress. The gap between reported figures and actual enemy losses was noted in internal analyses and dismissed as an unavoidable imprecision in a messy war. It was not imprecision. It was systematic inflation of a metric that had been chosen precisely because it could be inflated.

The deeper problem was that body count, even if perfectly accurate, measured the wrong thing. The relevant question was not how many NVA and Viet Cong soldiers had been killed but whether killing them at the achieved rate was degrading enemy capacity faster than North Vietnam could replace it. The replacement question required knowing the enemy's order of battle, recruiting capacity, training pipeline, and willingness to continue sustaining losses — all of which MACV consistently underestimated. A metric that measures tactical output without measuring strategic effect is not a measure of progress. It is a measure of activity. The attrition strategy produced enormous activity. It did not produce the crossover point, because the crossover point depended on assumptions about enemy behavior that the enemy consistently failed to validate.

onThisDay.headline: May Fourth Movement Demonstrations Begin in Beijing
onThisDay.body: On May 4, 1919, thousands of Chinese students demonstrated in Beijing against the Treaty of Versailles, which awarded Germany's Chinese concessions to Japan rather than returning them to China. The May Fourth Movement radicalized a generation of Chinese nationalists and intellectuals who would go on to found the Chinese Communist Party and shape the military forces that fought the subsequent decades of civil war.
